1408.title: Prayer and action
1408.howItsDone: Sikhs often offer an Ardas before a journey, an exam or a new venture and then set to work; the life is summed up as naam japo (remember the Name), kirat karo (earn honestly) and vand chhako (share).

segments.voice: Yesterday, asking and accepting: the Ardas, then the hukam, hands lifted, then left open. Your line was ask, then accept.

Before a long drive, before an exam, before a shop opens its doors for the first time, a Sikh family may stand together for an Ardas. Then somebody picks up the car keys. The prayer doesn't replace the driving. Nobody expects the car to steer itself because the prayer was heartfelt. Guru Arjan has a line that holds both halves in a single breath, and two old friends in the Granth argue it out.
screen: `AN ARDAS BEFORE THE DRIVE.` → `THEN, THE CAR KEYS.` → `BOTH HALVES.`

segments.voice: First, the line. In Gujri ki Var, Guru Arjan writes, in paraphrase: make the effort, and you live; earning, enjoy peace; meditating, meet the Lord; Nanak, the worry is gone. Udam karediaa jeeo toon. Effort, earning, meditation, all in one verse, and none of them cancels the others. Second, two friends. Among the saloks near the end of the Granth is a short exchange between two saints. In paraphrase: Trilochan says, my friend Namdev, you're caught up in the world; why are you busy printing cloth, instead of fixing your mind on the Lord? And Namdev answers: with your mouth, take the Lord's name; with hands and feet, do all your work; keep your mind with the Pure One. Namdev doesn't put the cloth down. The prayer rides along inside the work. Third, the short phrases. Sikhs sum up the life simply: naam japo, remember the Name; kirat karo, earn by honest work; vand chhako, share what you have. Prayer, work and sharing, braided, the way Namdev's mouth and hands kept moving together. Fourth, the order. Prayer comes first so the work comes from somewhere: humble, honest, aimed at the good of all. Then the work comes, so the prayer goes somewhere. A prayer for a hungry neighbor ends at the stove, with a pot on the flame and a knock on their door.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one task you keep circling, and sit still with it for a while. If you pray, offer it to God in your own words; if you don't, set an intention for how you want to do it: honestly, carefully, kindly. For the last few breaths, picture its very first physical step: opening the laptop, picking up the phone, putting on your shoes.
Prayer and action. In the Sikh pattern, prayer gives the work a source, and work gives the prayer somewhere to go. Today's word.
Your line: pray, then do. Namdev never put the cloth down. I'll be here tomorrow.

1409.title: Portrait of a Gurmukh
1409.howItsDone: Sikhs describe the gurmukh, one turned toward the Guru, as the ideal of the Sikh life: humble, truthful, content, serving others and remembering the Name; it is spoken of as something one grows into by grace and effort.

segments.voice: Yesterday, prayer and action: Namdev at his cloth, the Name on his lips. Your line was pray, then do.

Some people walk into a tense room and it settles a little. The arguing quiets. Somebody gets offered a chair. The kid in the corner gets noticed. They don't announce anything; nobody remembers what they said, only that things went better. The Sikh tradition has a word for a person living like that at their best: gurmukh. And for the opposite: manmukh. For weeks this path has taken the virtues one at a time. Today they sit together for a single portrait.

First, the word. Sikhs explain gurmukh as one whose face is turned toward the Guru, and manmukh as one turned toward their own mind. The difference isn't talent, or family, or how much scripture someone knows. It's direction. Second, the portrait. Gather the traits from these weeks and a likeness appears. Humble: strength that doesn't need to show. Truthful: in speech, and in conduct when nobody's checking. Content: at peace with what is, and still working. Serving: hands in the langar, at the shoe stand, with the dishes. Remembering: the Name under the breath, all through the day. Third, the text. A pauri of the Japji says, in paraphrase: through the Guru comes the sound of the Word; through the Guru comes wisdom; through the Guru, the One is found everywhere. Gurmukh naadan, gurmukh vedan. Here gurmukh is less a title than a doorway. Wisdom arrives by turning. Fourth, a portrait you grow into. Sikhs speak of becoming gurmukh, not of being born one, and they speak of it as grace and effort together. Nobody holds the whole likeness on a bad day. A portrait isn't a mirror that judges. It's a direction to face, again and again, like a sunflower turning through the day.
screen: `A FACE TURNED TOWARD THE GURU.` · `HUMBLE, TRUE, CONTENT, SERVING.` · `GURMUKH NAADAN, GURMUKH VEDAN.` · `A DIRECTION, NOT A MIRROR.` · then, large: `GROW INTO IT.`

segments.voice: Let the traits pass by slowly, one per breath: humble, truthful, content, serving, remembering. Notice which one feels farthest away today, not the easiest but the one that tugs, and breathe with it. Picture one moment where it could live, a meeting where someone else gets the credit, a dish you wash that isn't yours, and if you pray, hold that moment before God.
Portrait of a Gurmukh. One whose face is turned toward the Guru: humble, truthful, content, serving, remembering, and still growing. Today's word.
Your line: grow into it. Nobody is born holding the whole likeness. Go gently.

1410.title: Portrait of the Khalsa
1410.howItsDone: Sikhs who join the Khalsa take amrit in the amrit sanchar ceremony conducted by five initiated Sikhs, then keep the five Ks and the Sikh code of conduct (rehat); Sikhs who have not taken amrit are still Sikhs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the portrait of a gurmukh: humble, truthful, content, serving, remembering. Your line was grow into it.

A steel bowl of water and sugar. A double-edged sword stirring it while banis are recited. Five Sikhs, themselves already initiated, conduct the rite, and those coming forward drink the amrit and have it sprinkled on their eyes and hair. From that moment they belong to the Khalsa. Yesterday's portrait was the inner one, a face turned toward the Guru. Today the portrait gets a name, a code and a visible form.
screen: `A STEEL BOWL, A DOUBLE-EDGED SWORD.` → `THE AMRIT.` → `A NAME, A CODE, A FORM.`

segments.voice: First, pure. Sikhs say khalsa means pure. In a savaiya attributed to Guru Gobind Singh, in paraphrase: the one who remembers the ever-living light day and night, who brings no other but the One into the mind, in whose heart the full light shines, know that one as khaalas, pure. Purity here isn't a spotless record. It's a heart with one light in it. Second, brave. The Khalsa is remembered as saint-soldiers: ready to defend the weak, never to bully. Courage in this portrait is aimed outward, at someone else's safety. Third, disciplined. The Khalsa keep the five Ks, the daily prayers, and a code of conduct, the rehat, that rules out things like tobacco and adultery. It's a discipline you can see on a crowded street: the turban, the kara, the bearing. Fourth, generous. The hands that carry a kirpan also stir the pots in the langar and give a share of what they earn. And an honest note: not every Sikh has taken amrit. Sikhs who haven't are still Sikhs, and for some the Khalsa is a commitment grown toward slowly, when they're ready. Pure, brave, disciplined, generous.
screen: `PURE: ONE LIGHT IN THE HEART.` · `BRAVE: FOR SOMEONE ELSE'S SAFETY.` · `DISCIPLINED: THE REHAT.` · `GENEROUS: THE LANGAR POT.` · then, large: `KHALSA MEANS PURE.`

segments.voice: Let the traits pass, one per breath: pure, brave, disciplined, generous, and pick the one that asks the most of you today. Pure might mean one honest motive; brave, one hard sentence said kindly; disciplined, one habit kept when it's inconvenient; generous, one thing given before anyone asks. Breathe with your choice, and if you pray, offer that moment to God.
Portrait of the Khalsa. The initiated community of Sikhs: pure, brave, disciplined, generous, with one light in the heart. Today's word.
Your line: khalsa means pure. One light in the heart, nothing hidden behind it. That's today, done.

1411.title: Faith and the state
1411.hook: Sikhs hold different views on religion and politics; the Gurus spoke truth to rulers
1411.howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Nanak's hymns and saloks on rulers, including the Babarvani, as part of the Guru Granth Sahib and look to the Akal Takht in Amritsar as a seat of temporal authority; Sikhs differ on how directly faith should engage in politics.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Khalsa: pure, brave, disciplined, generous. Your line was khalsa means pure.

Kings are tigers, and their officials are dogs. That isn't a protest sign. It's a line of scripture, a salok of Guru Nanak kept in the Guru Granth Sahib. It says out loud, about the powerful, what the people under them might only whisper at home. The village clerk, the tax collector, the guard at the gate: the ones who knock at night. Guru Nanak doesn't flatter them, and he doesn't flatter the throne behind them either. Truth, spoken to rulers.
screen: `KINGS ARE TIGERS.` → `A LINE OF SCRIPTURE.` → `TRUTH TO RULERS.`

segments.voice: First, Guru Nanak's words. In the salok, in paraphrase: kings are tigers, their officials are dogs; they go and wake the sleeping to harass them. The servants of power wound people with their claws. Blunt language about rulers, with no single king named. A few weeks ago, this path heard the Babarvani, his hymns on an invasion, which call the invading host a wedding party of sin. The salok turns the same honesty on ordinary rule. Second, the throne facing the temple. Tradition says Guru Hargobind wore two swords, miri and piri, worldly authority and spiritual authority, and built the Akal Takht, the Throne of the Timeless One, facing the Harmandir Sahib. The message Sikhs draw from it: faith has something to say to power, and doesn't bow to it. Third, honest disagreement. Sikhs today hold different views on how faith and politics should meet. Some see miri-piri as a call to stay engaged in public life, as Sikhs, together. Others keep faith out of party politics and put it into service and conscience instead. Both draw on the same Gurus, and the tradition holds room for both. Fourth, what they share. Speaking truth to rulers isn't the same as wanting to rule. The Gurus' words name injustice plainly, without flattery and without hatred. It can be as large as a hymn about an invasion, or as small as one honest sentence at a city council, in an office, at a family table where one person's word is law.

segments.voice: Bring to mind a place where power sits over you, a boss, an office, a rule, a family elder, and ask whether one honest thing there needs saying. Don't draft a speech; find the one sentence and turn it over, breath by breath, until it's both true and kind. If you pray, ask for courage in your own words.

1412.title: The Granth's languages
1412.hook: Punjabi, saint-speech, Braj and Persian voices, all in one script
1412.howItsDone: Sikhs learn to read Gurmukhi, often in gurdwara classes, so they can read the Guru Granth Sahib themselves, and the hymns are sung in their original words whatever language they lean toward.

segments.voice: Yesterday, faith and the state: kings are tigers, and the Gurus spoke plainly to the powerful. Your line was truth to rulers.

Open the Guru Granth Sahib and the letters look steady from page to page: one script, Gurmukhi, running down the lines. Read it aloud, though, and the sound keeps shifting. One hymn rolls in the Punjabi of village fields. A few pages on, a verse leans toward Persian, the language of courts and clerks. Another carries the old speech of wandering saint-poets. Same letters, different voices. A child who has learned the alphabet can sound out every line, and still meet words that traveled a long way to get there.
screen: `ONE SCRIPT ON EVERY PAGE.` → `READ ALOUD, THE SOUND SHIFTS.` → `MANY VOICES, ONE ALPHABET.`

segments.voice: First, the mix. Readers who study the Granth hear Punjabi in it, and the shared poetic speech of north Indian saints that scholars call Sant Bhasha, along with Braj, Persian and Arabic words, and verses that lean toward Sanskrit. The Gurus sang to the people in front of them, and those people spoke in more than one way. Second, one example. In Raag Tilang, Guru Nanak opens a hymn with yak arj guftam, words a Persian speaker would recognize: one plea I make before you. In paraphrase, he asks the Creator to listen, and says this world is passing. A prayer in the language of the court, set among hymns in the language of the village. Third, other voices. The Granth also holds the hymns of bhagats, saints from outside the line of the Gurus. Kabir calls himself a weaver. Sheikh Farid's sloks keep a Punjabi sound of their own. Their words were kept in their own speech, not smoothed into one. Fourth, the script. All of it is written in Gurmukhi. Tradition says Guru Angad shaped the script so ordinary people could read the hymns for themselves, with no one standing between them and the Word. So a child in a gurdwara class on a Sunday morning can sound out Persian, Braj and Punjabi alike. The voices stay different. The letters stay the same.
screen: `MANY SPEECHES ON ONE PAGE.` · `YAK ARJ GUFTAM: ONE PLEA BEFORE YOU.` · `THE BHAGATS KEEP THEIR OWN VOICES.` · `ONE SCRIPT ANYONE CAN LEARN.` · then, large: `MANY TONGUES, ONE SCRIPT.`

segments.voice: On one breath, say softly, or only in your mind, Kartar, the Creator, the name Guru Nanak calls on in his Tilang hymn; on the next, Khuda, a name for God a Persian speaker would know, which the Granth uses too; on the next, Hari, a name from older Indian devotional verse, which the hymns use too. Let the three sounds sit together, pointing the same way. If you pray, let them be your prayer; if you don't, just notice how each one feels in the mouth.
The Granth's languages. Punjabi, Persian, Braj and the speech of the saints, held in a single script, Gurmukhi. Today's word.
Your line: many tongues, one script. Words that traveled far, in letters a child can learn. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1413.title: Why music
1413.hook: raga is theology: the Word must be felt, not only read
1413.howItsDone: In gurdwaras, the hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib are sung as kirtan, usually with harmonium and tabla, in the raga named at the head of each hymn, and the congregation often sings the refrain together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Granth's languages: Punjabi, Persian, Braj and the speech of the saints, in one alphabet. Your line was many tongues, one script.

The harmonium wheezes into its first note before anyone sings a word. Then the tabla comes in, soft at first, and a voice lifts a line from the Guru Granth Sahib, and the people sitting on the floor sing it back. In the gurdwara, the hymns are sung. A visitor might wonder why. If the words are holy, why not just read them out clearly, so nobody misses a syllable? The Sikh answer isn't that music makes the words prettier. It's closer to this: some things have to reach you through the ear and the chest before they reach the head.
screen: `THE HARMONIUM, THE TABLA, A VOICE.` → `WHY NOT JUST READ IT?` → `THROUGH THE EAR AND THE CHEST.`

segments.voice: First, look at how the book is built. After the opening prayers, the Granth is arranged by raga. Each hymn sits under a heading that names its musical mode before it names the Guru who wrote it. The book is ordered like a songbook, by mood, not by date or author. A raga isn't just a tune. It's a mood, a color, a time of day, and the hymn was meant to arrive inside it. Second, the first musician. Tradition says Guru Nanak traveled with a Muslim companion, Bhai Mardana, who played the rabab, a stringed instrument. The janamsakhis, the old story collections, tell of Nanak asking Mardana to play, and the hymn coming as song. From the start, as Sikhs tell it, the Word came with music under it. Third, the word for this singing: kirtan, singing the praise of God. Guru Arjan, in Raag Maru, says that in this dark age kirtan is foremost. Not a decoration. Foremost. Fourth, why it matters. You can read a line about longing and understand it. Sung in a raga made for longing, you meet it differently: in the breath, in the pause before the line comes back. Many Sikh teachers speak of the Word needing to be felt, not only parsed. Music slows you to the hymn's speed. It makes you repeat. It lets a room of strangers carry the same line together. A spoken sentence can slip past. A sung line comes around again.

Hum along on one low, easy note if you'd like, and if you pray, let the listening be the prayer.
Why music. Because the Granth is a songbook ordered by raga, and kirtan, singing the praise, carries the Word into the body. Today's word.

1414.title: Kesh as acceptance
1414.hook: uncut hair as trust in the body as given
1414.howItsDone: Sikhs who keep kesh leave their hair uncut, comb it with a kangha, and cover it, men usually with a turban and women with a turban or a scarf; initiated Sikhs keep it as one of the articles of the Khalsa.

segments.voice: Yesterday, why music: the Granth ordered by raga, and kirtan carrying the Word into the body. Your line was felt, not just read.

A small wooden comb, curved, with fine teeth, tucked into a knot of hair at the top of the head. That's the kangha, and it's there for kesh, hair that is never cut. A whole economy runs on changing how we look: trims, dyes, straighteners, filters on photos. Into that world, a Sikh walks with hair left as it grew, wrapped under a turban or a scarf. From outside, it can look like a rule about appearance. Sikhs tell it another way: a body left as it was given.
screen: `A SMALL WOODEN COMB.` → `HAIR THAT IS NEVER CUT.` → `A BODY LEFT AS GIVEN.`

segments.voice: Day three met kesh under the turban, and day one hundred thirty-nine said start where you are; today goes deeper. First, what kesh is. It's uncut hair, and for Sikhs who have taken amrit, the Khalsa initiation, it's one of the articles of faith they keep. The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, names cutting the hair among the things an initiated Sikh must not do. Other Sikhs keep their hair without having taken amrit, and some don't keep it; the gurdwara door is open to all of them. Second, a phrase from the Granth. In a hymn in Raag Maru, Guru Arjan describes a life of true devotion in the language of his Muslim neighbors, and one of his images is sabat surat: the form kept whole, with the turban on the head. Whole. Not edited. Third, why whole. Sikh teaching speaks of hukam, the divine order, and Guru Nanak's Japji says that by that order forms come into being. If the body came through that order, then leaving it uncut is a way of saying: I accept this as given. Not a better version. This one. Fourth, acceptance isn't neglect. The same tradition that keeps the hair uncut gives it a comb. Kesh is washed, combed, oiled, wrapped with care, and the turban is tied fresh. That's acceptance, not giving up: you don't fight the body or abandon it; you tend what you were given. Maybe the hardest idea here: the thing you'd most like to change about yourself could be met with a comb instead of a blade.
screen: `KESH: HAIR LEFT UNCUT.` · `SABAT SURAT: THE FORM KEPT WHOLE.` · `FORMS COME BY THE ORDER.` · `A COMB, NOT A BLADE.` · then, large: `AS GIVEN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one part of your body you've argued with, your hair, your height, a scar, a knee that complains on the stairs, and if it's easy to reach, rest a hand on it. Breathe in and let it be there without the argument; breathe out and say quietly, or only in your mind: as given. You don't have to love it today; just stop fighting it for a moment.
Kesh as acceptance. Uncut hair, kept whole and cared for, as trust in the body as it was given. Today's word.
Your line: as given. Washed, combed, wrapped with care, and left whole. See you again tomorrow.
